q: The first rule of performance work is
options: Measure, because programmers guess wrong about which line is slow with great consistency
why: Including the people who wrote the program, about their own program.

options: Time in the function itself, excluding what it called
why: A large `cumtime` with a small `tottime` means the work is underneath. Keep looking down.

q: `timeit` reports the best of many runs rather than the mean because
options: Noise only ever makes things slower, so the minimum is closest to the time the code needs
The mean is harder to compute
The first run is always fastest
why: It also repeats, which measures the steady state rather than the cold start.

q: Before profiling, the more important question is
options: How the cost grows with the input, because almost every emergency is an accidental quadratic
why: Run it on ten times the data and see whether the time goes up ten times or a hundred.

q: `if x in big_list` inside a loop is
options: Quadratic, and the fix is a set
why: The single most common performance bug in real Python.

q: Building a string with `+=` in a loop
options: Copies everything accumulated so far on each step, so the total is quadratic
why: `"".join(parts)` adds up the lengths, allocates once, and fills it.

options: Doing the work fewer times, or on less data
why: Those change the shape of the cost. A twenty percent speedup is a percentage; batching is a multiple.

options: One request per row where one request would have done
why: The tell in a profile is a large `cumtime`, a small `tottime`, and a very large call count.

options: Keeps a heap of size 3 and walks the input once, rather than ordering everything
why: The same family as `bisect` for search and `Counter.most_common`: a narrower question, a smaller cost.

q: `sum`, `sorted`, `any` and `join` are faster than a hand-written loop because
options: They run the loop in C rather than as interpreter steps
why: Which is also why the ceiling is low: when the loop itself is the cost, the loop has to leave Python.

q: `any(check(r) for r in rows)` against `any([check(r) for r in rows])`
options: The first short-circuits; the second builds the whole list, checking everything
The first is lazy but checks everything anyway
why: Which matters whenever the check costs something.

options: Regularly makes the large case worse, because the algorithm that wins at small n is the naive one
Works if the sample is random
why: Measure how each one grows, not which is faster on ten rows.

q: The number in a profile worth acting on is
options: The largest one you can change
The one with the most calls
why: A profile dominated by `socket.recv` is telling you to look at concurrency, not at optimisation.

options: Readability, paid by everybody who reads the code afterwards
why: Which is why the sequence ends with "if it is fast enough now, stop".

q: Reaching for `numpy`, Cython or Rust is right when
options: The profile says the bottleneck is Python's interpreter loop itself
why: Until then the problem is usually something you can fix in an afternoon.
